node.label: Anne McClintock
node.date_label: “Family Feuds: Gender, Nationalism and the Family” (1993) · Imperial Leather (1995) · Dangerous Liaisons: coedited collection (1997)
node.description: Analyzes nationalism through gendered access to political agency and the family images that make hierarchy appear natural. The selected opening of “Family Feuds” asks how women become symbolic bearers of national belonging while access to rights and resources remains uneven. Its family-trope discussion examines how national and imperial narratives turn social hierarchy and violent historical change into seemingly organic development. In a specifically named response to Edward Said, she retains his distinction between filiation and affiliation but argues that familial images persist inside new national, bureaucratic and imperial institutions. These are her situated historical interpretations, not universal facts established merely by the force of a theoretical formulation.

proposed_edges.relationship: Examines unequal national agency and the use of women as symbolic bearers of national belonging.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary pp. 61–63, with pp. 64–65 family/hierarchy context read in Wisconsin author-hosted scan text. General “all nations” formulations remain McClintock’s claims; no universal empirical certification or denial of women’s political action.

proposed_edges.relationship: Retains Said’s filiation/affiliation distinction while disputing a linear replacement of family relations by nonfamilial institutional orders.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Specifically named primary response, printed p. 64 with pp. 63–65 context. She argues that familial images were reinvented within national and imperial institutions. Said’s underlying passage is not newly collated and the critique is not generalized to all his work.
